slides.title: Chapter 5: The Levi-Civita Connection
slides.notes: Open the chapter by reminding students that they already know what a connection is in the abstract, but until now they had no preferred connection on a Riemannian manifold. The point of this chapter is to single out exactly one connection from the Riemannian metric and then to use it as the engine that drives geodesics, the exponential map, normal neighborhoods, and Fermi coordinates. Frame the whole arc as: metric chooses connection, connection chooses geodesics, geodesics chart the neighborhood.

slides.title: The Tangential Connection on Submanifolds
slides.notes: Walk through the construction explicitly. We sit inside a Euclidean ambient space, where directional differentiation is unambiguous. The trouble is that the derivative of a tangent vector field is no longer tangent to the submanifold, so we project orthogonally back to the tangent space. Emphasize two facts before moving on: the projection is metric-compatible because we are using the ambient inner product, and the result is symmetric because Euclidean differentiation is symmetric on coordinate vector fields. These two properties will reappear as the defining axioms of the Levi-Civita connection in the next slide.

slides.title: Fundamental Theorem of Riemannian Geometry
slides.notes: This is the central theorem of the chapter. Present it as a uniqueness-and-existence package: uniqueness comes first because it is forced by an algebraic manipulation, and existence comes second because we can read the Koszul formula as a definition. Stress the geometric reading of metric compatibility, namely that inner products do not drift under parallel transport, and the geometric reading of being torsion-free, namely that the connection does not twist coordinate frames. Both axioms are independent and together they leave no freedom.

slides.title: The Koszul Formula Forces Uniqueness
slides.notes: The Koszul formula is the workhorse of the existence-uniqueness proof. Walk students through the cyclic structure: the three permutations of X, Y, Z appear once each in the metric derivatives, and the three pairwise brackets appear once each among the structure terms. Once a student sees that the right-hand side depends only on the metric and the Lie bracket, they understand why the connection is forced. Mention that this is also a recipe: in any concrete chart, plug in coordinate frames and the formula becomes the Christoffel formula in the next slide.

slides.title: Christoffel Symbols in Terms of the Metric
slides.notes: This is the computational face of the theorem. The Christoffel symbols are not tensorial, but they are the only thing one has to differentiate vector fields in coordinates. Make sure students understand that the symmetry of the lower indices is equivalent to the torsion-free axiom, not an extra assumption. Mention that the same expression will reappear in geodesic equations, in the formula for the exponential map, and in normal coordinate computations later in the chapter.

slides.title: The Exponential Map at a Point
slides.notes: The exponential map is the geometric upgrade of the geodesic ODE. Every tangent vector at p selects one geodesic and the map records its position one unit of time later. Highlight the local diffeomorphism statement: at the origin the derivative is the identity, so a neighborhood of zero in the tangent space is identified with a neighborhood of p on the manifold. This is the doorway to normal coordinates and the linearization techniques used throughout Riemannian geometry.

slides.title: Normal Neighborhoods and Normal Coordinates
slides.notes: Normal coordinates are the most useful coordinate system in Riemannian geometry because they let students compute as if working in flat Euclidean space at the basepoint while still tracking curvature in higher derivatives of the metric. Make sure they remember the trade-off: simplification holds only at p, not in a neighborhood, and the second derivatives of g at p store the curvature data. Connect this to the notebook lab, which numerically demonstrates that radial paths from the origin really are unit-speed geodesics.

slides.title: Fermi Coordinates Along a Submanifold
slides.notes: Fermi coordinates are the submanifold version of normal coordinates. Replace the basepoint p by an embedded submanifold S, and replace radial geodesics by geodesics that leave S orthogonally. Highlight the structural reward: the metric is block-diagonal along S, so the geometry of S inside M decouples cleanly into intrinsic and extrinsic parts. This is the toolkit students will use for tubular neighborhoods and for computing second fundamental forms in later chapters.

slides.title: Geodesics in the Three Model Spaces
slides.notes: Use this slide as a comparative anchor. The same geodesic equation produces three qualitatively different families of curves once the metric is fixed. Stress that the formulas on the sphere and hyperbolic space involve circular and hyperbolic functions exactly because the curvatures are plus and minus one, while the Euclidean case has no curvature and so produces purely linear motion. Mention that these closed-form solutions are why the model spaces serve as comparison benchmarks throughout the rest of the book.

slides.title: What Chapter 5 Hands to Later Chapters
slides.notes: Close the chapter by stitching the parts together. The Levi-Civita connection is the unique tool that converts a Riemannian metric into a calculus on vector fields, and from that calculus we derived the exponential map, normal coordinates, Fermi coordinates, and the model-space geodesics. Each of these will be used immediately in the curvature chapter that follows, so this recap is also a forecast: the geodesic flow becomes the laboratory for curvature, and the comparison theorems will measure deviation from the three model spaces.
